value.overview: The Purple-throated Fruitcrow (Querula purpurata) is a distinctive cotinga of tropical American forests. It is a social, mostly black bird whose adult male has a conspicuous purple or wine-colored throat patch. Unlike many cotingas, it commonly lives and feeds in small family groups and has a cooperative breeding system. The species is usually found in forest canopies and midlevels, where it searches for fruit and large insects and gives varied, rough calls.
value.classification: The Purple-throated Fruitcrow belongs to the cotinga family, Cotingidae, within the order Passeriformes. Querula is a monotypic genus containing only this species.
value.identification: Adults are medium-sized, broad-bodied forest birds, generally about 28–30 cm long. Males are glossy black with a prominent dark purple to reddish-purple throat shield, while females and immature birds are duller and may lack a strongly developed throat patch. The bill is pale grayish or silvery, often with a darker tip. Its conspicuous throat, black plumage, arboreal habits, and noisy group behavior help distinguish it from other Costa Rican cotingas.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range in tropical America. In Central America it occurs from southeastern Nicaragua through the Caribbean lowlands of Costa Rica and Panama, with additional distribution on Panama’s Pacific side. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Caribbean slope and adjacent eastern lowlands, generally from sea level to about 500 m. It inhabits mature, lowland evergreen rainforest, especially the middle and upper canopy, and may be seen near forest edges, clearings, and gardens with forest connections.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, Purple-throated Fruitcrows remain in the Caribbean lowlands and eastern foothills throughout the year, although local movements may occur as birds follow fruit availability.
value.breeding: Purple-throated Fruitcrows breed cooperatively, with several adults helping to build, defend, incubate, and provision a nest. The nest is a shallow, loose platform or cup of sticks and fine twigs, usually placed in a tree fork well above the ground. Clutches generally contain one egg. Breeding is associated with the local wet season in several parts of the range; Costa Rican observations indicate nesting can occur during the wetter months, but a precise national breeding calendar is not well documented.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms the main part of the diet, supplemented by large insects and other arthropods. Birds usually forage in small groups in the forest’s middle and upper levels, taking fruit while perched or making short sallies from exposed branches. Adults commonly deliver insects to nestlings, particularly during early development. By carrying and later releasing seeds away from feeding trees, the species may contribute to forest seed dispersal.
value.behavior: This is a highly social and vocal cotinga, commonly traveling in small groups of roughly three to eight birds. Groups may include adults, immature birds, and helpers, and occasionally associate with mixed-species flocks. Birds move through the canopy and midstory while calling with mewing, rising, or raspy sounds. Males display by spreading the throat shield and shivering the tail. Groups also cooperate in nest defense against predators.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered very large, but it is believed to be decreasing.
